Free Offer of the Gospel
FREE AW-fur uhv thuh GOS-puhl
noun (gospel proclamation)
From offer, Latin offerre, to present or hold forth; the gracious presenting of Christ to all who hear the gospel, with a sincere call to come.

See also: Free Offer of the Gospel

📖 Biblical Definition

The free offer of the gospel is the well-meant proclamation in which Christ, with all His benefits, is sincerely held forth to every hearer, with a true command to repent and believe and a genuine promise of salvation to all who come. The offer is universal in its proclamation, though redemption is particular in its accomplishment. God calls indiscriminately: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters" (Isa 55:1), and Christ Himself cries, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28). The Spirit and the bride say, "Come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Rev 22:17). This sincere call stands in full harmony with particular redemption, for the offer is to be made to all, while the saving power of it belongs to the elect through effectual calling. Against the cold error of hyper-Calvinism, which forbids the free offer and will not press Christ upon sinners, this dictionary confesses that the gospel is to be preached to every creature, that God is not the author of any man's ruin, and that the warrant to believe rests not on secret election but on the open command and promise of God in the gospel.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The free offer is the sincere holding-forth of Christ to every hearer, with a true command to believe and a real promise to all who come. It is consistent with particular redemption, for the offer is universal while saving power is the elect's. It is denied by hyper-Calvinism, which this dictionary rejects.

expand to see more

FREE OFFER, noun. The sincere and well-meant presentation of Christ and His salvation to all who hear the gospel.

It includes a genuine command to repent and believe and a real promise of life to all who come.

"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

It requires the preacher to press Christ upon every sinner; it forbids the withholding of the gospel from any.

It stands consistent with definite atonement, the offer being universal and the saving call effectual in the elect.

📖 Key Scripture

Isa 55:1 — "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."

Matt 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Rev 22:17 — "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

Ezek 33:11 — "Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Two errors flank the truth: hyper-Calvinism denies the well-meant offer, while Arminianism grounds it in a universal atonement and the autonomous free will of man.

expand to see more

Hyper-Calvinism, fearing to compromise sovereignty, refuses to offer Christ to all and will only address the offer to sensible sinners or the awakened. This chills evangelism, hides the warrant to believe, and contradicts the apostolic pattern of preaching repentance to every creature. On the opposite hand, Arminianism makes the offer rest on a universal redemption and a will free to turn itself, so that the decisive cause of salvation lies in the sinner. Both miss the biblical balance.

Scripture holds the offer and the decree together without strain. God sincerely commands all to come and truly promises life to all who do, while the effectual call savingly draws the elect. The preacher is to spread the table wide and beseech men to be reconciled to God; the secret election is the Lord's business, the open offer is ours. This is the apostolic temper, and the church neglects it to her own coldness.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The offer is rooted in the gospel imperatives of Scripture, where Christ is held forth and sinners are commanded to come.

expand to see more

The Hebrew imperative of Isa 55:1, leku, "come ye," opens the invitation to all the thirsty.

The Greek deute in Matt 11:28, "come," is Christ's own summons to the heavy-laden.

The word offer, from Latin offerre, means to hold forth or present freely.

The phrase "whosoever will" in Rev 22:17 marks the universal sweep of the gospel call.

Ezek 33:11 grounds the sincerity of the call in God's declared pleasure that the wicked turn and live.

Usage

"He pressed the free offer upon every soul in the room, beseeching them to come to Christ at once."

"The free offer of the gospel and the doctrine of particular redemption are not enemies but companions."

"Hyper-Calvinism silenced the free offer in that pulpit, and the congregation grew cold and small."
